Module 01 / Physics 2

Fluids: start with a force diagram

Density, pressure, hydraulics, and floating bodies.

Topics in this module
Density, relative density, and unit conversionsPressure and the hydrostatic derivationAtmospheric, gauge, absolute, and connected-column casesPascal's principle and hydraulic displacementArchimedes' principle: derive it before choosing a volumeFloating, sinking, and identifying unknown densitySource tables, pressure units, and the two air examplesMissing companion pressure and buoyancy problemsWorked applications: models, calculations, and interpretation

A fluid can flow. Liquids and gases are fluids. Fluid statics studies equilibrium; fluid dynamics studies motion. In the molecular model, gas particles are widely separated and compressible. A liquid has a definite volume but takes its container's shape. The hydrostatic formulas below require a stationary fluid, not an accelerating flow.

Density, relative density, and unit conversions

Density measures mass per volume. Relative density compares two densities and has no unit. Use the fluid density in buoyancy calculations, not the object's density.

ρ=mV,m=ρV,V=mρ,w=mg=ρVg,SG=ρρwater.\rho=\frac mV,\quad m=\rho V,\quad V=\frac m\rho,\quad w=mg=\rho Vg,\quad SG=\frac{\rho}{\rho_{water}}.ρ=Vm​,m=ρV,V=ρm​,w=mg=ρVg,SG=ρwater​ρ​.

For a composite body, divide the total mass by the total external volume. For separate parts with additive volumes, use ρavg=∑m∑V\rho _{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{\sum m}{\sum V}ρavg​=∑V∑m​. A hollow object's average density includes its empty interior. Water is about 1000 kgm31000\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}1000m3kg​ in the classroom model. Convert 1gcm3\frac{1 g}{\mathrm{cm}^{3}}cm31g​ to 1000 kgm31000\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}1000m3kg​. Also use 1L=10−3 m31 L = 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^{3}1L=10−3m3, 1 mL=1 cm31\,\mathrm{mL} = 1\,\mathrm{cm}^{3}1mL=1cm3, and 1 cm3=10−6 m31\,\mathrm{cm}^{3} = 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}^{3}1cm3=10−6m3. Squaring and cubing conversion factors is essential.

Worked example — primary p. 10. A room measures 4.0×5.0×3.0 m4.0 \times 5.0 \times 3.0\,\mathrm{m}4.0×5.0×3.0m. With ρair=1.20 kgm3\rho _{\mathrm{air}} = 1.20\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}ρair​=1.20m3kg​, V=60 m3V = 60\,\mathrm{m}^{3}V=60m3. Therefore m=1.20×60=72 kgm = 1.20 \times 60 = 72\,\mathrm{kg}m=1.20×60=72kg. Its weight is 72×9.81=706.32 N72 \times 9.81 = 706.32\,\mathrm{N}72×9.81=706.32N. Mass and weight have different units.

Pressure and the hydrostatic derivation

Pressure is normal force per area: P=F⊥AP = \frac{F_{\perp}}{A}P=AF⊥​​. One pascal equals one Nm2\frac{N}{m^{2}}m2N​. Rearrange to F⊥=PAF_{\perp} = PAF⊥​=PA or A=F⊥PA = \frac{F_{\perp}}{P}A=PF⊥​​. Pressure is a scalar; the force on each wall points perpendicular to that wall. A static fluid cannot sustain a shear stress.

Derivation. Isolate a vertical fluid column of area A and depth h. The downward forces are P0AP_{0} AP0​A and its weight ρAhg\rho AhgρAhg. The upward force is PbottomA. Equilibrium gives:

PbA−P0A−ρAhg=0⇒Pb=P0+ρgh.P_bA-P_0A-\rho Ahg=0\Rightarrow P_b=P_0+\rho gh.Pb​A−P0​A−ρAhg=0⇒Pb​=P0​+ρgh.

The area cancels. This explains why pressure at a given depth does not depend on container shape. Equal pressure at equal depth requires the same connected, stationary fluid under the same surface conditions.

ΔP=ρgh,h=ΔPρg,ρ=ΔPgh,F=(P0+ρgh)A.\Delta P=\rho gh,\quad h=\frac{\Delta P}{\rho g},\quad \rho=\frac{\Delta P}{gh},\quad F=(P_0+\rho gh)A.ΔP=ρgh,h=ρgΔP​,ρ=ghΔP​,F=(P0​+ρgh)A.

Pressure differences across a wall use the pressure on BOTH sides. Do not multiply an absolute pressure by area when the question asks the net force against outside air. For nonconstant density, the general vertical relation is dPdz=−ρ(z)g\frac{dP}{dz} = - \rho \left( z \right) gdzdP​=−ρ(z)g; integrate instead of assuming ρgh\rho ghρgh.

Worked example — diver, primary p. 17. At 20 m20\,\mathrm{m}20m in freshwater, Pgauge=1000×9.8×20=196,000 PaP_{\mathrm{gauge}} = 1000 \times 9.8 \times 20 = 196{,}000\,\mathrm{Pa}Pgauge​=1000×9.8×20=196,000Pa. Add 101,300 Pa101{,}300\,\mathrm{Pa}101,300Pa for an absolute pressure of 297,300 Pa297{,}300\,\mathrm{Pa}297,300Pa. The statement “pressure due to water” means the gauge contribution here.

Worked example — two liquids, primary p. 19. At 3.00 m3.00\,\mathrm{m}3.00m and g=9.81 ms2g = 9.81\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}^{2}}g=9.81s2m​, freshwater gives 130,730 Pa130{,}730\,\mathrm{Pa}130,730Pa absolute. Seawater with ρ=1030\rho = 1030ρ=1030 gives 131,612.9 Pa131{,}612.9\,\mathrm{Pa}131,612.9Pa. Their difference is 882.9 Pa882.9\,\mathrm{Pa}882.9Pa, because the same atmospheric term cancels.

Atmospheric, gauge, absolute, and connected-column cases

Pabs=Patm+Pg,Pg=Pabs−Patm.P_{abs}=P_{atm}+P_g,\quad P_g=P_{abs}-P_{atm}.Pabs​=Patm​+Pg​,Pg​=Pabs​−Patm​.

The slides use 1 atm≈101.3 kPa=760 torr≈760 mmHg1\,\mathrm{atm} \approx 101.3\,\mathrm{kPa} = 760\,\mathrm{torr} \approx 760\,\mathrm{mmHg}1atm≈101.3kPa=760torr≈760mmHg. Gauge pressure can be negative; absolute pressure cannot be negative. Vacuum devices do not create a pulling pressure. A pressure difference lets the higher-pressure surroundings push inward.

For a manometer, start at a known pressure. Add ρgΔh\rho g\Delta hρgΔh when moving DOWN through a fluid. Subtract it when moving UP. Keep each fluid's density separate. Set pressures equal at the same level only within the same connected fluid. For multiple stationary layers, Pbottom=Ptop+∑ρighiP_{\mathrm{bottom}} = P_{\mathrm{top}} + \sum \rho_{i} gh_{i}Pbottom​=Ptop​+∑ρi​ghi​.

Worked example — companion p. 6 type. A closed water column's gas interface is 0.60 m0.60\,\mathrm{m}0.60m below an open water surface. Pgas=101,300+1000×9.81×0.60=107,186 PaP_{\mathrm{gas}} = 101{,}300 + 1000 \times 9.81 \times 0.60 = 107{,}186\,\mathrm{Pa}Pgas​=101,300+1000×9.81×0.60=107,186Pa, about 1.058 atm1.058\,\mathrm{atm}1.058atm. A different interface height reverses the sign. The drawing, not the word “closed,” decides the height contribution.

Pascal's principle and hydraulic displacement

An applied pressure change travels through a confined fluid. At equal piston elevations and neglecting friction, ΔP1=ΔP2\Delta P_{1} = \Delta P_{2}ΔP1​=ΔP2​:

F1A1=F2A2,F2=F1A2A1=F1(r2r1)2.\frac{F_1}{A_1}=\frac{F_2}{A_2},\quad F_2=F_1\frac{A_2}{A_1}=F_1\left(\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^2.A1​F1​​=A2​F2​​,F2​=F1​A1​A2​​=F1​(r1​r2​​)2.

Derive the distance relation. Conservation of incompressible fluid volume gives A1d1=A2d2A_{1} d_{1} = A_{2} d_{2}A1​d1​=A2​d2​. Thus d2d1=A1A2\frac{d_{2}}{d_{1}} = \frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}d1​d2​​=A2​A1​​. Multiplying by the force ratio gives F1d1=F2d2F_{1} d_{1} = F_{2} d_{2}F1​d1​=F2​d2​: force multiplication is not energy creation. For unequal piston heights, include the hydrostatic pressure difference before applying the force balance.

Worked example — primary p. 23. A 10,000 N10{,}000\,\mathrm{N}10,000N load sits on a piston of radius 1.00 m1.00\,\mathrm{m}1.00m. The smaller radius is 0.050 m0.050\,\mathrm{m}0.050m. Required input force: 10,000(0.0501.00)2=25 N10{,}000 \left( \frac{0.050}{1.00} \right)^{2} = 25\,\mathrm{N}10,000(1.000.050​)2=25N. A diameter ratio gives the same squared ratio if both inputs are diameters.

Worked example — companion p. 7. Diameters 5 cm5\,\mathrm{cm}5cm and 25 cm25\,\mathrm{cm}25cm give an area ratio of 25. An input of 100 N100\,\mathrm{N}100N produces 2500 N2500\,\mathrm{N}2500N ideally. The large piston moves only 125\frac{1}{25}251​ of the smaller piston's distance.

Archimedes' principle: derive it before choosing a volume

Pressure at a submerged block's bottom exceeds the pressure at its top. For constant area A, the net upward fluid force is (Pbottom−Ptop)A=ρfg(hbottom−htop)A\left( P_{\mathrm{bottom}} - P_{\mathrm{top}} \right) A = \rho_{f} g \left( h_{\mathrm{bottom}} - h_{\mathrm{top}} \right) A(Pbottom​−Ptop​)A=ρf​g(hbottom​−htop​)A. Since AΔh=VdisplacedA\Delta h = V_{\mathrm{displaced}}AΔh=Vdisplaced​:

FB=ρfgVdisp.F_B=\rho_f gV_{disp}.FB​=ρf​gVdisp​.

This relation uses the volume of displaced fluid. For a fully submerged impermeable body, it equals the object's external volume. For partial immersion, it does not equal the whole object volume. A fluid's pressure gradient produces buoyancy even without a free surface immediately beside the object.

For a hanging object in equilibrium, T+FB−mg=0T + F_{B} - mg = 0T+FB​−mg=0, so T=mg−FBT = mg - F_{B}T=mg−FB​. Apparent weight equals that tension. If a light object is tied DOWN, FB−mg−T=0F_{B} - mg - T = 0FB​−mg−T=0, so T=FB−mgT = F_{B} - mgT=FB​−mg. Choose the sign from the diagram.

Worked example — primary p. 32 type. A 2.00 kg2.00\,\mathrm{kg}2.00kg brass block has density 8700 kgm38700\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}8700m3kg​ and is fully submerged in water. V=28700=2.299×10−4 m3V = \frac{2}{8700} = 2.299 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^{3}V=87002​=2.299×10−4m3. FB=2.255 NF_{B} = 2.255\,\mathrm{N}FB​=2.255N. Its upward-string tension is 19.62−2.255=17.365 N19.62 - 2.255 = 17.365\,\mathrm{N}19.62−2.255=17.365N. The density is the chosen brass-table value; a different supplied value changes the result.

Worked example — companion pp. 9–10. A 0.10 m0.10\,\mathrm{m}0.10m cube of wood has density 700 kgm3700\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}700m3kg​. V=0.001 m3V = 0.001\,\mathrm{m}^{3}V=0.001m3, mg=6.867 Nmg = 6.867\,\mathrm{N}mg=6.867N, and FB=9.81 NF_{B} = 9.81\,\mathrm{N}FB​=9.81N. A bottom string must pull downward with 2.943 N2.943\,\mathrm{N}2.943N. A negative “upward tension” would indicate the wrong assumed string direction.

Floating, sinking, and identifying unknown density

For free floating equilibrium, FB=mgF_{B} = mgFB​=mg. With m=ρobjectVtotalm = \rho _{\mathrm{object}}V_{\mathrm{total}}m=ρobject​Vtotal​:

VsubVtotal=ρobjectρf,ρf=ρobjectVtotalVsub.\frac{V_{sub}}{V_{total}}=\frac{\rho_{object}}{\rho_f},\quad \rho_f=\rho_{object}\frac{V_{total}}{V_{sub}}.Vtotal​Vsub​​=ρf​ρobject​​,ρf​=ρobject​Vsub​Vtotal​​.

This fraction must lie between zero and one. If the average object density exceeds the fluid density, a freely floating equilibrium with partial immersion is impossible. A sinking object still has an upward buoyant force; that force is simply insufficient to balance its weight. Neutral buoyancy means equal average densities, not zero buoyancy.

Worked example — primary p. 34. One-third of a person's volume is above the surface, so two-thirds is submerged. With average density 970 kgm3970\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}970m3kg​, fluid density: 970(23)=1455 kgm3\frac{970}{\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)} = 1455\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}(32​)970​=1455m3kg​. The printed 1460 is a rounded value. The assumed 3 m33\,\mathrm{m}^{3}3m3 is only a convenient volume ratio, not a realistic measured body volume.

Take note. Primary p. 12 labels density with Pa; its unit must be kgm3\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{m^{3}}m3kg​. Floating formulas require equilibrium without an extra vertical support force. Do not use them for a block held underwater by a string.

Derivation extension — weighing an unknown solid. Measure the weight Wair in air, then the apparent weight Wsub while fully submerged. Neglect air buoyancy and string mass. The difference is the fluid buoyancy: Wair−Wsub=ρfgVW_{\mathrm{air}} - W_{\mathrm{sub}} = \rho_{f} gVWair​−Wsub​=ρf​gV. Meanwhile Wair=ρobjectgVW_{\mathrm{air}} = \rho _{\mathrm{object}} gVWair​=ρobject​gV. Divide the equations to remove both g and V:

ρobject=ρfWairWair−Wsub.\rho_{object}=\rho_f\frac{W_{air}}{W_{air}-W_{sub}}.ρobject​=ρf​Wair​−Wsub​Wair​​.

For Wair=12.0 NW_{\mathrm{air}} = 12.0\,\mathrm{N}Wair​=12.0N and Wsub=8.0 NW_{\mathrm{sub}} = 8.0\,\mathrm{N}Wsub​=8.0N in water, density: 1000(12)(12−8)=3000 kgm3\frac{1000 \left( 12 \right)}{\left( 12 - 8 \right)} = 3000\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}(12−8)1000(12)​=3000m3kg​. A smaller apparent weight means a larger buoyant force. This formula does not apply unchanged to an object resting on the bottom.

Worked extension — a layered column. An open tank holds 0.20 m0.20\,\mathrm{m}0.20m of oil, density 800 kgm3800\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}800m3kg​, above 0.30 m0.30\,\mathrm{m}0.30m of water. Gauge pressure at the bottom is 800(9.81)(0.20)+1000(9.81)(0.30)=4512.6 Pa800 \left( 9.81 \right) \left( 0.20 \right) + 1000 \left( 9.81 \right) \left( 0.30 \right) = 4512.6\,\mathrm{Pa}800(9.81)(0.20)+1000(9.81)(0.30)=4512.6Pa. A small horizontal bottom hatch of area 0.010 m20.010\,\mathrm{m}^{2}0.010m2, exposed to air underneath, feels a net downward force of 45.126 N45.126\,\mathrm{N}45.126N. Atmospheric pressure cancels across the hatch. For a tall vertical hatch, pressure varies over its area; use F=∫PdepthdAF = \int P_{\mathrm{depth}} dAF=∫Pdepth​dA, not the pressure at its lowest point everywhere.

These are the source's classroom values. Temperature and composition affect real densities. The brass example below uses the explicit 8700 kgm38700\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}8700m3kg​ value from p. 9.

Why a fluid has pressure — companion pp. 3–4. Molecular motion and interactions transfer momentum to container walls. Gravity creates a vertical pressure gradient, but it is not the only cause of pressure. Gas molecules still collide with walls in weightlessness. Over a small laboratory height, a gas's gravitational pressure change can be small; atmospheric pressure changes substantially over larger heights. Internal and external pressure partly balance around the body, so atmospheric pressure does not act as an unopposed inward force everywhere.

Relative-density check. Steel: SG=78001000=7.80SG = \frac{7800}{1000} = 7.80SG=10007800​=7.80. Brass: SG=87001000=8.70SG = \frac{8700}{1000} = 8.70SG=10008700​=8.70. Wood: SG=5001000=0.500SG = \frac{500}{1000} = 0.500SG=1000500​=0.500. Relative density has no kgm3\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{m^{3}}m3kg​ unit because the density units cancel.

Air in a room: distinguish the primary and companion problems

Sources: Primary p. 10; companion p. 2. Find: The air mass, then its weight.

  1. Use the primary dimensions 4.0×5.0×3.0 m4.0 \times 5.0 \times 3.0\,\mathrm{m}4.0×5.0×3.0m. Their product is 60 m360\,\mathrm{m}^{3}60m3.
  2. Use its 20°C air density: m=ρV=1.20(60)=72 kgm = \rho V = 1.20 \left( 60 \right) = 72\,\mathrm{kg}m=ρV=1.20(60)=72kg.
  3. Calculate weight separately: W=mg=72(9.81)=706.32 NW = mg = 72 \left( 9.81 \right) = 706.32\,\mathrm{N}W=mg=72(9.81)=706.32N.
  4. Use the companion dimensions 4.0×6.0×2.5 m4.0 \times 6.0 \times 2.5\,\mathrm{m}4.0×6.0×2.5m. Their product also equals 60 m360\,\mathrm{m}^{3}60m3.
  5. Use the companion's 0°C table: m=1.29(60)=77.4 kgm = 1.29 \left( 60 \right) = 77.4\,\mathrm{kg}m=1.29(60)=77.4kg, which rounds to 77 kg77\,\mathrm{kg}77kg.

Check. The volumes agree, but the selected air densities differ. The two mass answers therefore do not contradict each other.

Pressure on the submarine

  1. Calculate the water contribution: ΔP=1030(9.8)(300)=3,028,200 Pa\Delta P = 1030 \left( 9.8 \right) \left( 300 \right) = 3{,}028{,}200\,\mathrm{Pa}ΔP=1030(9.8)(300)=3,028,200Pa.

Pressure at the closed end of the water tube

Source: Companion p. 6. Given: Open surface height 1.00 m1.00\,\mathrm{m}1.00m; closed-end height 0.40 m0.40\,\mathrm{m}0.40m above the same reference. Surface pressure is 1 atm1\,\mathrm{atm}1atm.

  1. Find the depth below the open surface: h=1.00−0.40=0.60 mh = 1.00 - 0.40 = 0.60\,\mathrm{m}h=1.00−0.40=0.60m.
  2. Move down through water, so add the hydrostatic term.
  3. Calculate Pclosed=101,300+1000(9.81)(0.60)=107,186 Pa\begin{aligned}P_{\mathrm{closed}} &= 101{,}300 + 1000 \left( 9.81 \right) \left( 0.60 \right) \\&= 107{,}186\,\mathrm{Pa}\end{aligned}Pclosed​​=101,300+1000(9.81)(0.60)=107,186Pa​
  4. Divide by 101,300 to obtain 1.0581 atm1.0581\,\mathrm{atm}1.0581atm, about 1.06 atm1.06\,\mathrm{atm}1.06atm.
  5. Change the surface pressure to 1.50 atm1.50\,\mathrm{atm}1.50atm for the follow-up question. The water contribution stays 0.0581 atm0.0581\,\mathrm{atm}0.0581atm.
  6. Obtain a new closed-end pressure of 1.5581 atm1.5581\,\mathrm{atm}1.5581atm, about 1.56 atm1.56\,\mathrm{atm}1.56atm.

Check. Pascal's principle transfers the added 0.50 atm0.50\,\mathrm{atm}0.50atm without changing the depth difference. The word “closed” does not make the pressure zero.

  1. Write the common gauge pressure: ΔP=F1A1=F2A2\Delta P = \frac{F_{1}}{A_{1}} = \frac{F_{2}}{A_{2}}ΔP=A1​F1​​=A2​F2​​.

A fully submerged block: buoyancy, apparent weight, and sinking

Source: Companion p. 9. Given: Displaced volume 0.020 m30.020\,\mathrm{m}^{3}0.020m3; water density 1000 kgm31000\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}1000m3kg​; block weight 250 N250\,\mathrm{N}250N. Use g=9.8 ms2g = 9.8\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}^{2}}g=9.8s2m​.

  1. Calculate FB=ρfgV=1000(9.8)(0.020)=196 NF_{B} = \rho_{f} gV = 1000 \left( 9.8 \right) \left( 0.020 \right) = 196\,\mathrm{N}FB​=ρf​gV=1000(9.8)(0.020)=196N upward.
  2. Compare forces: the weight exceeds buoyancy by 250−196=54 N250 - 196 = 54\,\mathrm{N}250−196=54N.
  3. If released without support, the block accelerates downward initially. It sinks.
  4. If an upper string holds the block at rest, the string tension is 54 N54\,\mathrm{N}54N.

Check. The block still has buoyancy while sinking. “It sinks” does not mean FB=0F_{B} = 0FB​=0.

Complete the 2 kg2\,\mathrm{kg}2kg brass-block solution

Source: Primary p. 32, using the 8700 kgm38700\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}8700m3kg​ brass value on p. 9. Use g=9.81 ms2g = 9.81\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}^{2}}g=9.81s2m​.

  1. Find the external volume: V=mρbrass=28700=2.29885×10−4 m3V = \frac{m}{\rho _{\mathrm{brass}}} = \frac{2}{8700} = 2.29885 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^{3}V=ρbrass​m​=87002​=2.29885×10−4m3.
  2. Use that volume as the displaced-water volume because the block is fully submerged.
  3. Calculate FB=1000(9.81)V=2.25517 NF_{B} = 1000 \left( 9.81 \right) V = 2.25517\,\mathrm{N}FB​=1000(9.81)V=2.25517N upward.
  4. Calculate the true weight: mg=2(9.81)=19.62 Nmg = 2 \left( 9.81 \right) = 19.62\,\mathrm{N}mg=2(9.81)=19.62N downward.
  5. Write vertical equilibrium: T+FB−mg=0T + F_{B} - mg = 0T+FB​−mg=0.
  6. Solve T=19.62−2.25517=17.3648 NT = 19.62 - 2.25517 = 17.3648\,\mathrm{N}T=19.62−2.25517=17.3648N upward.

Value check. If a question instead supplies 8600 kgm38600\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}8600m3kg​ from p. 8, FB≈2.2814 NF_{B} \approx 2.2814\,\mathrm{N}FB​≈2.2814N and T≈17.3386 NT \approx 17.3386\,\mathrm{N}T≈17.3386N. State which density you use.

Worked solution↳

Why an iceberg is mostly underwater

Source: Companion p. 11. Given: Ice density 917 kgm3917\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}917m3kg​; seawater density 1030 kgm31030\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}1030m3kg​. Assume free floating equilibrium.

  1. Set FB=mgF_{B} = mgFB​=mg: ρseagVsub=ρicegVtotal\rho _{\mathrm{sea}} gV_{\mathrm{sub}} = \rho _{\mathrm{ice}} gV_{\mathrm{total}}ρsea​gVsub​=ρice​gVtotal​.
  2. Cancel g and divide by ρseaVtotal\rho _{\mathrm{sea}}V_{\mathrm{total}}ρsea​Vtotal​.
  3. Calculate VsubVtotal=9171030=0.890291\frac{V_{\mathrm{sub}}}{V_{\mathrm{total}}} = \frac{917}{1030} = 0.890291Vtotal​Vsub​​=1030917​=0.890291.
  4. Express the submerged fraction as 89.0% and the exposed fraction as 11.0%.

Check. The fraction is below one because ice is less dense than seawater. Do not apply this equilibrium fraction to the tied-down wood block.

Choose the correct force balance. Free floating: FB=mgF_{B} = mgFB​=mg. Upper support: T+FB=mgT + F_{B} = mgT+FB​=mg. Bottom tether: FB=mg+TF_{B} = mg + TFB​=mg+T. Start with the diagram before selecting an equation.

Worked solution↳

The bottom-tethered wood block, step by step

Source: Companion p. 10. Given: A 10 cm10\,\mathrm{cm}10cm cube, wood density 700 kgm3700\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}700m3kg​, and water density 1000 kgm31000\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}1000m3kg​. Use g=9.81 ms2g = 9.81\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}^{2}}g=9.81s2m​.

  1. Convert the side to 0.10 m0.10\,\mathrm{m}0.10m and calculate V=(0.10)3=0.001 m3V = \left( 0.10 \right)^{3} = 0.001\,\mathrm{m}^{3}V=(0.10)3=0.001m3.
  2. Find the block's mass: m=700(0.001)=0.700 kgm = 700 \left( 0.001 \right) = 0.700\,\mathrm{kg}m=700(0.001)=0.700kg.
  3. Find its weight: W=0.700(9.81)=6.867 NW = 0.700 \left( 9.81 \right) = 6.867\,\mathrm{N}W=0.700(9.81)=6.867N downward.
  4. Find buoyancy when fully submerged: FB=1000(9.81)(0.001)=9.810 NF_{B} = 1000 \left( 9.81 \right) \left( 0.001 \right) = 9.810\,\mathrm{N}FB​=1000(9.81)(0.001)=9.810N upward.
  5. Draw the string pulling downward toward its bottom attachment.
  6. Set FB−W−T=0F_{B} - W - T = 0FB​−W−T=0, giving T=9.810−6.867=2.943 NT = 9.810 - 6.867 = 2.943\,\mathrm{N}T=9.810−6.867=2.943N.

Check. Releasing the string leaves a net upward force initially. The block rises until a smaller displaced volume permits floating equilibrium.

Worked applications: models, calculations, and interpretation

These worked examples apply the module concepts. Each example states its conditions, explains the model, and shows the complete working.

Worked application 1: A tether below a buoyant body

A sealed rigid body is completely submerged. Buoyancy exceeds its weight. A string attached to the bottom holds it at rest.

The force balance determines the tension in the bottom tether.

  1. Identify all forces. The bottom tether pulls downward. Weight is downward; buoyancy is upward.

  2. Choose upward positive.

∑Fy=FB−mg−T=0\sum F_y=F_B-mg-T=0∑Fy​=FB​−mg−T=0
  1. Rearrange.
T=FB−mg>0T=F_B-mg>0T=FB​−mg>0
  1. Check the geometry. An upper string could not provide this required downward force. Attachment location is part of the problem.

Result: T=FB−mgT=F_B-mgT=FB​−mg

Worked application 2: A stone leaves a floating boat

A dense stone is carried in a boat floating on a still-water tank. The stone is then placed on the tank bottom. The boat stays afloat. Ignore absorption and volume changes.

The comparison determines the water-level change when the stone moves from the floating boat to the tank bottom.

  1. Count the stone’s contribution while carried.
Vbefore=msρwV_{\mathrm{before}}=\frac{m_s}{\rho_w}Vbefore​=ρw​ms​​
  1. Count it after sinking.
Vafter=msρsV_{\mathrm{after}}=\frac{m_s}{\rho_s}Vafter​=ρs​ms​​
  1. Use the density condition.
ρs>ρw ⟹ Vafter<Vbefore\rho_s>\rho_w\ \Longrightarrow\ V_{\mathrm{after}}<V_{\mathrm{before}}ρs​>ρw​ ⟹ Vafter​<Vbefore​
  1. Interpret the tank. The boat’s own weight contribution remains. The reduced total displacement lowers the level.

Result: It decreases.

Worked application 3: Depth and buoyancy

The same rigid sealed block is moved deeper while remaining fully submerged in an incompressible liquid of constant density. Its volume does not change.

The comparison explains buoyancy at different depths for the same fully submerged rigid block.

  1. Compare top and bottom pressures.
Pb−Pt=ρg(hb−ht)P_b-P_t=\rho g(h_b-h_t)Pb​−Pt​=ρg(hb​−ht​)

  1. Hold the relevant quantities fixed. The block’s height, volume, and fluid density do not change.

  2. Use displaced volume.

FB=ρgVdispF_B=\rho gV_{\mathrm{disp}}FB​=ρgVdisp​
  1. State the limit. A compressible body or a liquid whose density changes with depth needs a different analysis.

Result: It remains unchanged.

Worked application 4: Pressure across a hatch

A small flat hatch is horizontal, so all its points have the same depth. Water is on one side and a pressurized gas is on the other.

The pressure difference across the hatch determines its net force.

  1. Choose a force direction. Take the water-to-gas direction as positive.

  2. Add both signed forces.

Fnet=+PwA−PgAF_{\mathrm{net}}=+P_wA-P_gAFnet​=+Pw​A−Pg​A

  1. Check the sign. A negative result means the net force points from the gas side toward the water.

  2. Check the pressure model. For a tall vertical hatch, pressure varies with depth; a single-depth value cannot be applied to the whole hatch without justification.

Result: The pressure difference across the hatch: Fnet=(Pw−Pg)AF_{\mathrm{net}}=(P_w-P_g)AFnet​=(Pw​−Pg​)A.

Worked application 5: Hydraulics: diameter is not area

An ideal incompressible hydraulic lift has an output piston with three times the input piston’s diameter. Ignore piston weights and height differences.

The piston area ratio connects the output force and travel to the input force and travel.

  1. Convert diameter ratio to area ratio.
A2A1=(D2D1)2=9\frac{A_2}{A_1}=\left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right)^2=9A1​A2​​=(D1​D2​​)2=9
  1. Apply equal pressure.
F1A1=F2A2\frac{F_1}{A_1}=\frac{F_2}{A_2}A1​F1​​=A2​F2​​
  1. Apply volume conservation.
A1d1=A2d2A_1d_1=A_2d_2A1​d1​=A2​d2​
  1. Check ideal work.
F1d1=F2d2F_1d_1=F_2d_2F1​d1​=F2​d2​

Result: Force ×9; travel ÷9.

Worked application 6: Two fluid layers and a hatch

An open tank has a 0.30 m-thick oil layer above water. A small horizontal hatch is 0.40 m below the oil–water interface. Both the top liquid surface and the outside of the hatch are at the same atmospheric pressure. Oil density is 800 kg/m³; water density is 1000 kg/m³; hatch area is 0.020 m². The calculation determines the net water-side force magnitude. Use g=9.81 m s−2g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}g=9.81ms−2.

  1. Choose the pressure reference. The matching atmospheric terms cancel across the hatch.

  2. Add the two hydrostatic contributions.

ΔP=ρogho+ρwghw\Delta P=\rho_o gh_o+\rho_w gh_wΔP=ρo​gho​+ρw​ghw​
  1. Substitute layer by layer.
ΔP=800(9.81)(0.30)+1000(9.81)(0.40)=6278.4 Pa\Delta P=800(9.81)(0.30)+1000(9.81)(0.40)=6278.4\,\mathrm{Pa}ΔP=800(9.81)(0.30)+1000(9.81)(0.40)=6278.4Pa
  1. Convert pressure difference into force. Both layers contribute to the pressure at the hatch.
F=ΔPA=6278.4(0.020)F=\Delta PA=6278.4(0.020)F=ΔPA=6278.4(0.020)
  1. State the result.
125.568 N125.568\,\mathrm N125.568N

Result: 125.568 N125.568\,\mathrm N125.568N

Worked application 7: A floating block with cargo

A rigid block has volume 0.010 m³ and average density 600 kg/m³. It floats in freshwater of density 1000 kg/m³. A 2.0 kg load is placed on top without touching the water. The calculation determines the fraction of the block volume submerged after loading.

  1. Find the block mass.
mb=ρbV=600(0.010)=6.0 kgm_b=\rho_bV=600(0.010)=6.0\,\mathrm{kg}mb​=ρb​V=600(0.010)=6.0kg
  1. Balance the full supported weight.
ρwgVsub=(mb+mL)g\rho_wgV_{\mathrm{sub}}=(m_b+m_L)gρw​gVsub​=(mb​+mL​)g
  1. Find displaced volume.
Vsub=6.0+2.01000=0.0080 m3V_{\mathrm{sub}}=\frac{6.0+2.0}{1000}=0.0080\,\mathrm{m^3}Vsub​=10006.0+2.0​=0.0080m3
  1. Divide by the block volume. The result is below one, so the stated floating state is possible.
f=0.00800.010=0.80f=\frac{0.0080}{0.010}=0.80f=0.0100.0080​=0.80
  1. State the result.
0.80.80.8

Result: 0.80.80.8

Worked application 8: A bottom-tether force

A sealed 0.0040 m³ body has mass 2.0 kg and is fully submerged in freshwater. A tether to the bottom holds it at rest. Water density is 1000 kg/m³. The calculation determines the tether tension magnitude using g=9.81 m s−2g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}g=9.81ms−2.

  1. Find buoyancy.
FB=1000(9.81)(0.0040)=39.24 NF_B=1000(9.81)(0.0040)=39.24\,\mathrm NFB​=1000(9.81)(0.0040)=39.24N
  1. Find weight.
mg=2.0(9.81)=19.62 Nmg=2.0(9.81)=19.62\,\mathrm Nmg=2.0(9.81)=19.62N
  1. Apply upward-positive equilibrium.
FB−mg−T=0F_B-mg-T=0FB​−mg−T=0
  1. Isolate the downward tether magnitude. A positive downward tension is consistent with a body that would otherwise rise.
T=39.24−19.62T=39.24-19.62T=39.24−19.62
  1. State the result.
19.62 N19.62\,\mathrm N19.62N

Result: 19.62 N19.62\,\mathrm N19.62N

Worked application 9: Hydraulic force and displacement

An ideal lift uses piston diameters 2.0 cm and 10.0 cm. An input force of 120 N moves the small piston down 0.25 m. Ignore weights and elevation differences. The calculation determines the rise of the large piston.

  1. Find the area ratio.
A2A1=(10.02.0)2=25\frac{A_2}{A_1}=\left(\frac{10.0}{2.0}\right)^2=25A1​A2​​=(2.010.0​)2=25
  1. Use displaced-volume equality.
A1d1=A2d2⟹d2=d125A_1d_1=A_2d_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_2=\frac{d_1}{25}A1​d1​=A2​d2​⟹d2​=25d1​​
  1. Substitute the input travel. The force is multiplied by 25, but the travel is divided by 25.
d2=0.2525d_2=\frac{0.25}{25}d2​=250.25​
  1. Check work consistency.
F2=3000 N,120(0.25)=3000(0.010)=30 JF_2=3000\,\mathrm N,\quad 120(0.25)=3000(0.010)=30\,\mathrm JF2​=3000N,120(0.25)=3000(0.010)=30J
  1. State the result.
0.01 m0.01\,\mathrm m0.01m

Result: 0.01 m0.01\,\mathrm m0.01m

Worked application 10: Apparent weight identifies density

A uniform object weighs 30 N in air and has an apparent weight of 18 N while fully submerged in water. Ignore air buoyancy. Water density is 1000 kg/m³. The calculation determines the object’s density.

  1. Identify the buoyant force.
FB=W−T=30−18=12 NF_B=W-T=30-18=12\,\mathrm NFB​=W−T=30−18=12N
  1. Write weight and buoyancy for the same volume.
W=ρoVg,FB=ρwVgW=\rho_oVg,\qquad F_B=\rho_wVgW=ρo​Vg,FB​=ρw​Vg
  1. Eliminate volume and gravity.
ρo=ρwWW−T\rho_o=\rho_w\frac{W}{W-T}ρo​=ρw​W−TW​
  1. Substitute. The density exceeds water’s density, consistent with needing an upward support string.
ρo=10003012\rho_o=1000\frac{30}{12}ρo​=10001230​
  1. State the result.
2500 kg m−32500\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}2500kgm−3

Result: 2500 kg m−32500\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}2500kgm−3

Worked application 30: A block across a liquid interface · model and interpretation

A rigid block of volume V=0.006 m3V=0.006\,\mathrm{m^3}V=0.006m3 and mass m=5.4 kgm=5.4\,\mathrm{kg}m=5.4kg straddles two deep immiscible liquids. The upper liquid has density 800 kg m−3800\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}800kgm−3; the lower liquid has density 1000 kg m−31000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}1000kgm−3. Fraction f=0.2f=0.2f=0.2 of the block volume lies in the lower liquid. The rest lies in the upper liquid. An upper support holds the block at rest. Ignore surface tension; use g=9.81 m s−2g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}g=9.81ms−2.

Removing the support changes the equilibrium position; the lower-liquid displaced volume controls the buoyancy increase.

  1. Identify what stays fixed. Add buoyancy from each displaced liquid. The upper support supplies any remaining upward force.

  2. Add the two displaced-fluid weights.

FB=gV[ρ1(1−f)+ρ2f]=49.4424 NF_B=gV[\rho_1(1-f)+\rho_2f]=49.4424\,\mathrm NFB​=gV[ρ1​(1−f)+ρ2​f]=49.4424N
  1. Balance all vertical forces.
T+FB−mg=0 ⇒ T=mg−FBT+F_B-mg=0\ \Rightarrow\ T=mg-F_BT+FB​−mg=0 ⇒ T=mg−FB​
  1. Apply the conclusion. Increasing the lower-liquid fraction raises the displaced-fluid weight.

Result: The original buoyancy is below the weight; the lower liquid increases buoyancy as its displaced share grows.

m=W/g,ρb=m/Vm=W/g,\quad \rho_b=m/Vm=W/g,ρb​=m/V

A uniform rectangular raft has volume 0.4 m³, horizontal top area 1 m², and material density 400 kg m−3400\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}400kgm−3. It carries a 100 kg load in freshwater of density 1000 kg m−31000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}1000kgm−3. The load stays dry. Ignore waves, tilt, and water absorption. Use g=9.81 m s−2g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}g=9.81ms−2. The calculation determines the submerged volume fraction.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. A freely floating raft displaces water whose mass equals the raft-plus-load mass.

  2. Include the raft mass.

mtotal=ρrV+mL=400(0.4)+100=260 kgm_{\rm total}=\rho_rV+m_L=400(0.4)+100=260\,\mathrm{kg}mtotal​=ρr​V+mL​=400(0.4)+100=260kg
  1. Use the floating-force balance.
ρwgVdisp=mtotalg ⇒ Vdisp=0.26 m3\rho_wgV_{\rm disp}=m_{\rm total}g\ \Rightarrow\ V_{\rm disp}=0.26\,\mathrm{m^3}ρw​gVdisp​=mtotal​g ⇒ Vdisp​=0.26m3
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
f=Vdisp/V=0.26/0.4f=V_{\rm disp}/V=0.26/0.4f=Vdisp​/V=0.26/0.4

  1. Check the physical result. The fraction is below one, so the stated dry-top floating condition is possible.

  2. State the result.

Result: 0.650.650.65

Worked application 60: Load capacity and freeboard · model and interpretation

A uniform rectangular raft has volume 0.6 m³, horizontal top area 1.5 m², and material density 400 kg m−3400\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}400kgm−3. It carries a 160 kg load in freshwater of density 1000 kg m−31000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}1000kgm−3. The load stays dry. Ignore waves, tilt, and water absorption. Use g=9.81 m s−2g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}g=9.81ms−2.

The freeboard comparison uses the same extra dry load in denser water.

  1. Identify what stays fixed. A freely floating raft displaces water whose mass equals the raft-plus-load mass.

  2. Include the raft mass.

mtotal=ρrV+mL=400(0.6)+160=400 kgm_{\rm total}=\rho_rV+m_L=400(0.6)+160=400\,\mathrm{kg}mtotal​=ρr​V+mL​=400(0.6)+160=400kg
  1. Use the floating-force balance.
ρwgVdisp=mtotalg ⇒ Vdisp=0.4 m3\rho_wgV_{\rm disp}=m_{\rm total}g\ \Rightarrow\ V_{\rm disp}=0.4\,\mathrm{m^3}ρw​gVdisp​=mtotal​g ⇒ Vdisp​=0.4m3
  1. Apply the conclusion. The added displaced volume is added mass divided by fluid density.

Result: The freeboard decreases by a smaller amount than in freshwater.
